WHAT SCRIPTURE SAYS
What Scripture says of him
"In the year that Tartan came unto Ashdod, (when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him,) and fought against Ashdod, and took it". Isaiah 20:1

At that time the LORD told Isaiah to loose the sackcloth from his loins and put off his shoes, "walking naked and barefoot", as a sign that "the king of Assyria" would lead the Egyptians and the Ethiopians away captive. Isaiah 20:2–4
DEALINGS
Dealings with God's people
The sign was aimed at those who looked to Ethiopia and Egypt for help: "such is our expectation, whither we flee for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria". Isaiah 20:5–6
EVENTS
Wars, works and turning points

DATES DIFFER
When was it?

SCRIPTURE'S NUMBERS
No years given
Scripture names Sargon once and gives no dates for him (Isa 20:1).
SKINNER (1896–98)
THE BABYLONIAN CHRONICLE AND EPONYM LIST
No years given[72][74]
He took the throne on the twelfth of Tebet after Shalmaneser's death; Sennacherib took the throne on the twelfth of Ab, 705 BC.
Another name of Sennacherib
the Geneva Bible notes (1599); John Gill (1748–63)

The Geneva note says "The Hebrews write that Sennacherib was so called". Gill: Sargon "is generally thought to be the same with Sennacherib, since Tartan was one of his generals" (2 Kings 18:17). Isaiah 20:1 2 Kings 18:17 [43][58]
Shalmaneser, Sennacherib or Esarhaddon
Matthew Poole (1683–85)
Poole, noting that kings often had several names, offers three candidates: Shalmaneser, Sennacherib, or Esarhaddon, whose name he thought might be shortened to Sargon. Isaiah 20:1 [63]
A king of his own, Sennacherib's father
J. Skinner (1896–98); R. W. Rogers (1912)

Skinner: the guess of a few scholars that Sargon was "an intermediate king" had been "amply verified by the progress of Assyriology"; he reigned 722–705. Rogers writes that Sennacherib, Sargon's son, took the throne in the month Sargon died. Isaiah 20:1 [53][82]

WHAT SCRIPTURE DOES NOT SAY
Scripture names Sargon once and records nothing else he did.
Isaiah 20 does not say whether Judah joined Ashdod's revolt.
Scripture does not connect Sargon with the fall of Samaria; that claim is in his own inscriptions.
Scripture does not say how Sargon died.
IDENTIFICATIONS THIS PAGE RELIES ON

Scholars' viewScripture names Sargon only in Isaiah 20:1. Older writers often took the name for another name of Sennacherib or of another king; the Assyrian records show him as a king in his own right, the father of Sennacherib (see the question below). Isaiah 20:1 [53][82]

Scholars' view"Tartan" is a title, the Assyrian commander next to the king. The site's person record for Tartan joins the Tartan of Isaiah 20:1 with Sennacherib's Tartan (2 Kings 18:17); Ellicott's commentary says the two "may, or may not" be the same man. Isaiah 20:1 2 Kings 18:17 [12]
